facts.value: No general daily OT; manufacturing establishments must pay 1.5x for hours over 10/day (and over 40/week generally)
facts.summary: Oregon follows the federal 40-hour weekly overtime rule, but additionally requires daily overtime (1.5x) for employees in manufacturing establishments who work more than 10 hours in a single day.
facts.notes: Manufacturing daily OT is an Oregon addition beyond federal FLSA. Oregon has no statewide salary threshold above the federal white-collar exemption; verify against current OAR 839-020.

facts.summary: Oregon's standard minimum wage is $15.55/hour effective July 1, 2026; the Portland metro rate is $16.80 and the non-urban (rural) county rate is $14.55, all well above the federal $7.25.
facts.notes: Oregon uses a three-tier geographic system. Rates adjust each July 1 based on CPI. Confirm the exact 2026-2027 figures ($15.55 standard / $16.80 Portland metro / $14.55 non-urban) on the BOLI minimum-wage schedule page before publishing.

facts.summary: Beyond the federal protected classes, Oregon law prohibits employment discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, marital status, family relationship, uniformed service status, and age (18 and older, broader than the federal 40+).
facts.notes: Oregon also protects race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, and retaliation (which overlap with federal). Age protection begins at 18 rather than 40.

facts.summary: Oregon's core anti-discrimination protections apply to employers with one or more employees, far lower than the federal 15-employee threshold under Title VII/ADA.
facts.notes: Coverage varies by protected class: 1+ employees for most classes; disability and pregnancy accommodation require 6+ employees.

facts.value: Disability discrimination and reasonable-accommodation duties apply to employers with 6 or more employees; pregnancy-related accommodation also required
facts.summary: Oregon requires reasonable accommodation for disability for employers with six or more employees (lower than the federal ADA's 15), and separately mandates reasonable accommodation for pregnancy, childbirth, and related conditions.
facts.notes: Six-employee threshold for disability is lower than federal ADA (15). Verify pregnancy accommodation specifics under the Oregon Employer Accommodation for Pregnancy Act.

facts.value: Prohibits retaliation against employees who in good faith report suspected violations of state/federal law or who oppose unlawful practices
facts.summary: Oregon law bars employers from taking adverse action (discharge, demotion, suspension, pay cuts) against workers who in good faith report or oppose conduct they reasonably believe violates state or federal law.
facts.notes: ORS 659A.199 covers private employers; ORS 659A.203 covers public and nonprofit employers. Worker need not be correct, only hold a good-faith belief. Remedies include reinstatement, back pay, and attorney fees via ORS 659A.885.

facts.value: 1 year for most claims; up to 5 years for claims under ORS 659A.030, 659A.082, 659A.112, 659A.370, or 243.323
facts.summary: An employee generally has 1 year from the alleged unlawful practice to file either an administrative complaint with BOLI or a civil action in court. Oregon's Workplace Fairness Act extends that deadline to 5 years -- for both a BOLI complaint and a civil lawsuit -- for incidents occurring on or after September 29, 2019, if the claim falls under ORS 659A.030 (race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, national origin, marital status, or age discrimination), 659A.082, 659A.112 (disability), 659A.370, or 243.323. Other unlawful-employment-practice claims keep the general 1-year deadline; confirm which limitations period applies to the specific claim before relying on either figure.
facts.notes: The 5-year window (added by 2019 SB 726, the Workplace Fairness Act) applies to BOTH the BOLI administrative complaint (ORS 659A.820) and a civil action (ORS 659A.875) -- it is not limited to civil suits -- but only for the enumerated statutes (243.323, 659A.030, 659A.082, 659A.112, 659A.370), which cover most but not all discrimination/retaliation claim types. Any unlawful-employment-practice claim outside that list is subject to the general 1-year deadline in both forums. Verify the applicable statute for the specific claim before relying on a deadline.

facts.value: Due end of next business day if fired/laid off; within 5 business days or next payday (whichever first) if quit without 48 hrs notice; on last day if 48+ hrs notice
facts.summary: Oregon sets strict final-paycheck deadlines and imposes penalty wages of up to 8x the employee's daily rate for each day wages remain unpaid, capped at 30 days.
facts.notes: Penalty-wage safe harbor caps liability if unpaid wages are paid within 12 days of written notice. Federal law has no comparable final-pay timing rule.

facts.value: Equal pay required for work of comparable character across protected classes; claims must be filed within 1 year
facts.summary: Oregon's Equal Pay Act requires equal compensation for work of comparable character regardless of protected class (broader than the federal Equal Pay Act's sex-only scope) and bars asking about salary history.
facts.notes: Covers race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, national origin, marital status, veteran status, disability, and age. Equal Pay Act claims carry a 1-year statute of limitations under ORS 652.230.

facts.summary: Oregon applies a 6-year statute of limitations (under ORS 12.080) to claims for unpaid regular wages under the state wage-collection law.
facts.notes: BOLI's published case-law digest states: 'the statute of limitations for wage claims for regular wages is six years' (citing ORS 12.080), rejecting a shorter-period defense in In the Matter of Brown's Architectural Sheetmetal, Inc., 35 BOLI 68 (2016). Separate, shorter deadlines apply to civil penalty wages (ORS 652.150, notice/30-day accrual) and the Oregon Equal Pay Act (1 year, ORS 652.230 - see the equalPay fact).
